Genetic Genealogy solving cold cases

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.........how genetics and family trees are solving crimes

Unique Selling Point:
Genetic Genealogy is a new tool investigators are using to solve cold case crimes

Summary:
There is a new crime solving tool on the rise. A company has pioneered a technique to use genetic genealogy, a forensic technique for tracking down suspects through their family trees, to help close more than 70 cold cases since May last year. In 2018, criminal investigators in the United States embraced the tool, solving decades-old cold cases and some fresh crimes.

Further information:
In the insert we will use interviews with the company that pioneered the technique -- Parabon Nanolabs, as well as a South African genealogist. We will also use a South African case study -- somebody who used genetic genealogy to trace a distant/unknown relative.

More info:

US truck driver gets life for DNA-based murder conviction
Updated / Thursday, 25 Jul 2019 09:23

A US truck driver, implicated by his DNA and family tree in a double murder more than 30 years after the crime, has been sentenced to life imprisonment in the first case using a revolutionary investigative technique.

William Talbott II was convicted at the end of June of killing two young Canadians, Jay Cook, 20, and his girlfriend Tanya Van Cuylenborg, 18, in 1987 near Seattle.

The evidence for his conviction was found with "genetic genealogy", which involves making DNA matches with distant relatives.

Cook was suffocated to death, with a pack of cigarettes stuffed into his throat, and Van Cuylenborg died of a gunshot wound to the head.

They had driven to Seattle on 18 November 1987 to pick up an item for Cook's father at a heating company.

Police said they took a ferry from Victoria to Port Angeles that afternoon and their last known whereabouts was in Bremerton later that night where they bought a ticket for the Seattle ferry.

On 24 November, Van Cuylenborg's partially clothed body was found in a ditch in Skagit County.

The following day the couple's van was found locked up and abandoned in a car park in Bellingham. Cook's body was found in Snohomish County on 26 November 1987.

After decades of unsuccessful searching, Seattle police finally arrested Talbott, 56, in May 2018, though he had not raised suspicions until then.

Snohomish County detective Jim Scharf, who led the investigation, credited genetic genealogy for Talbott's capture.

The technique first made headlines in 2018 after it was used to find the suspected "Golden State Killer", who is blamed for 12 murders and more than 50 rapes dating back to the mid-1970s.

In both cases, as well as at least 70 others that have been solved since, DNA found at the crime scenes was compared with the database at GEDmatch, a free genealogy website.

The website allows users to post DNA test results and then generates a list of people with similar genomes, enabling users to find distant relatives.


The database also allowed police officers to search through people with similar genetic profiles to DNA found at crime scenes.

Tracing back through family trees and isolating common relatives can lead investigators to a suspect.

In addition to helping solve more than 70 cases, which had gone unsolved for years, some of the suspects identified through the process were convicted after pleading guilty.

But this is the first case in which a trial was organised, despite Talbott maintaining his innocence.

After his sentencing yesterday, he continued to claim his innocence and said he intended to appeal the sentence.

GENETICS,SCIENCE & SOCIETY
Crime solvers embraced genetic genealogy


The Golden State killer case was just the beginning
BY TINA HESMAN SAEY 8:32AM, DECEMBER 17, 2018



Every week, Ellen Greytak checks DNA profiles in a genealogy database. She’s not searching for long-lost relatives. She’s out to find family members of unknown assailants in rape and murder cases.
Greytak is director of bioinformatics at Parabon NanoLabs in Reston, Va. Since May, the company has used genetic genealogy, a forensic technique for tracking down suspects through their family trees, to help close more than a dozen cases nationwide.

In 2018, criminal investigators in the United States embraced the tool, solving decades-old cold cases and some fresh crimes.

More than 12 million Americans have jumped on the consumer genetic testing bandwagon, sending spit samples to companies like 23andMe or AncestryDNA to learn about health risks and to explore family origins (SN: 6/23/18, p. 26). People who’ve had their DNA tested and want to find relatives tested by a different company can upload their results to a public database called GEDMatch.

Now GEDMatch is being used to locate rape and murder suspects. In April, Sacramento police arrested Joseph James DeAngelo as a suspect in the Golden State Killer case (SN Online: 4/29/18). DeAngelo, a former police officer, is accused of committing about 50 rapes and 12 murders from 1974 to 1986.

Police found DNA matches in GEDMatch to multiple third cousins of DeAngelo. Building out the suspect’s family tree eventually led investigators to DeAngelo. A few weeks after DeAngelo’s arrest, Parabon identified William Earl Talbott II as a suspect in a 1987 double murder of a young Canadian couple in Snohomish County, Wash. (SN: 6/23/18, p. 11). Since then, suspects in 16 other cases have been arrested after genetic genealogy searches.

Script:


GENETIC GENEALOGY AND COLD CASES SCRIPT
AUDIO
V/O:
In 1987 Jay Cook and Tanya Van Cuylenborg were just a happy, young couple from Canada, madly in love. But their lives were cut short by a brutal murder which would go unsolved for 31 years…Until a chance DNA connection unmasked their killer.
LINK:
Forensic investigators have also been using DNA analysis, but mainly to identify perpetrators by comparing a suspect’s DNA to a database.
V/O:
It was first introduced into in forensics in in the mid 1980’s, and has been used in the same way for more than 30 years.

But in the last two years, a dramatic new breakthrough in forensic in science has changed how investigators can use DNA samples to track perpetrators and solve decades old cold cases.

Dr Ellen Greytak of Parabon Nanolabs in Virginia, USA says this new method of analysis moves the investigation to the next level.
Ellen:
But now we have brought in these new techniques that can actually analyse the DNA and tell detectives something they did not know before. Instead of saying “Well, it is not that guy”, it tells them a description of that person.
V/O:
And last year, we put this incredible development to the test. Could they using just a sample of DNA, predict what a person actually looks like - their ethnicity, height and maybe even their eye color?

We sent our own Devi Sankaree Govender’s DNA samples to Dr Greytak for a prediction.
Devi:
And this is the predicted picture aged at about 25. And I must say, I did look like that.
LINK
But apart from Phenotyping as this is known, Dr Greytak and her colleagues knew that DNA profiles can also be used for something else.
V/O:
Instead of only using it to look for what makes a person unique, it can also be used to show the common genetic characteristics between individuals… in other words, determining who a person is related to…
In the last decade, this use of DNA analysis has become very popular with the general public.

As more affordable DNA tests have come onto the market, millions of people around the world have had their DNA analysed to trace their family lineage.

Gladys van Wyk, a restaurant owner in Johannesburg…did that.
Derek:
How did you go about it?

Gladys:
So, I ordered a kit from My Heritage. They sent me a kit with a little tube inside. You take your spit, you put it inside the tube and then you send it back to them. In a couple of weeks you will have your results.
V/O:
Gladys’ DNA results showed that her ancestors came from Central and North Africa as well as Spain, India and even Russia and Sweden...

Then she took it a step further, uploading her results to a website called GEDMatch – where millions of DNA profiles are compared … and people sharing the same genetic components are matched as relatives.

Gladys discovered she has several cousins she knew nothing about – some in South Africa and even one in Russia.
V/O:
Jaco Strauss is a genealogist from Somerset West.
JACO:
You see in America quite an explosion. In 2018 the number of ancestry test at home exceeded all previous tests done over all the previous years combined. So that is a massive explosion. We unfortunately do not see the same explosion in South Africa but we do have a steady stream of people testing and the number of results we can work with increase over time.
V/O:
Now with a public database consisting of millions of DNA profiles, Dr Greytak and her colleagues decided to explore this further… leading to the next major breakthrough in forensic science.

By using this DNA database, which identifies the pieces of DNA related people share, they could find the relatives of unknown perpetrators of crimes.
LINK 4:
The number of pieces you share with somebody else can tell you a lot about the genetic relationship between you and the other person.
V/O:
It can show you how closely you are related – siblings, or first or second or third cousins.

By uploading the unknown DNA sample to GEDMatch, they could trace all the people who shared the same genetic makeup and with a match, they could establish that all the relatives led back to the perpetrator…
Ellen:
And we can then use that information to try and figure out who an unknow person is based on who they are related to.
V/O:
They do this by using the DNA matches as the basis for exploration and with traditional genealogy, they draw a family tree of the known person.

Because the unknown offender is part of this family tree, they use it to determine their identity.

The experiment worked.
Ellen:
The first cold case we solved through genetic genealogy was in Washington State and this was a 31-year-old cold case. A murder of this young couple from Canada and they had come down in van and were found murdered a few days later having been murdered, and this person, this perpetrator had been living his life for 31 years.
V/O:
On the scene of the crime the murderer had left some DNA, so they already knew he was a male.
LINK 5:
Then Dr Greytak and her collegues uploaded the murderer’s DNA profile onto GEDMatch. They found two distant relatives of the murderer.
Ellen:
We saw two second cousins, two people at approximately second cousin level who were not related to each other.
V/O:
This means the two people they found, were from two unrelated families. But the murderer was related to both these families.
LINK 6:
Now it may sound complicated, but the only way the murderer could be related to both these two unrelated families was if he was the result of a union between individuals from the respective families.
V/O:
So Parabon’s lead genealogist started to analyse the family trees of both families, looking for evidence of a union or marriage between the two families.
Ellen:
CC our lead genealogist came back and said “I found him. I know who this guy is.”
V/O:
She had indeed found evidence of a marriage between the two families. Such a union would have passed pieces of DNA from both families on to the murderer, giving rise to the specific DNA profile found on the scene.
Ellen:
So, in this case we find a marriage between these two family trees. That means that the children of that marriage are the second cousins to both matches in the database and they are the only people in these trees who are related to both matches. And in this case, if there is only one male child, we know that person has to be our unknown person on interest.
V/O:
The company could then give the investigators a name. The police traced the man, followed him and collected a cup he had been drinking from.
LINK
They tested the DNA on the cup and it was a perfect match to the DNA collected on the crime scene
V/O:
And so, 31 years after he murdered 2 young people in cold blood, William Talbott was arrested last year. A few weeks ago he was convicted of first degree murder. It was the first case ever where genetic genealogy had been used to identify and convict a murderer.

Since May last year, Parabon has solved more than 70 cold cases through genetic genealogy.

Michael Whyte was arrested for murdering Darlene Krashoc 1987 in Colrado.

In Seattle in Washington State police solved a 52 year old open murder case after the DNA from a Frank Wypych matched the DNA of the person who had killed 20-year-old Susan Galvin in 1967.

This technique of tackling cold cases is still not a viable option in South Africa because so few South African profiles are available for cross-referencing.
Link:
But while not yet useful for solving cold cases here, genetic genealogy can help South Africans to trace long lost family and even relatives they never knew about.
Derek:
Any other names crop up there?

Gladys:
Yes! Klaassen, Esterhuizen, Kampher, van Wyk, Smit with a T, Smith with a TH, Rossouw.

Derek:
Quite a few.

Gladys:
Quite a few non-African ancestors.

Derek: Any other names crop up there? Gladys: Yes! Klaassen, Esterhuizen, Kampher, van Wyk, Smit with a T, Smith with a TH, Rossouw. Derek: Quite a few. Gladys: Quite a few non-African ancestors.

More info: US truck driver gets life for DNA-based murder conviction Updated / Thursday, 25 Jul 2019 09:23 A US truck driver, implicated by his DNA and family tree in a double murder more than 30 years after the crime, has been sentenced to life imprisonment in the first case using a revolutionary investigative technique. William Talbott II was convicted at the end of June of killing two young Canadians, Jay Cook, 20, and his girlfriend Tanya Van Cuylenborg, 18, in 1987 near Seattle. The evidence for his conviction was found with "genetic genealogy", which involves making DNA matches with distant relatives. Cook was suffocated to death, with a pack of cigarettes stuffed into his throat, and Van Cuylenborg died of a gunshot wound to the head. They had driven to Seattle on 18 November 1987 to pick up an item for Cook's father at a heating company. Police said they took a ferry from Victoria to Port Angeles that afternoon and their last known whereabouts was in Bremerton later that night where they bought a ticket for the Seattle ferry. On 24 November, Van Cuylenborg's partially clothed body was found in a ditch in Skagit County. The following day the couple's van was found locked up and abandoned in a car park in Bellingham. Cook's body was found in Snohomish County on 26 November 1987. After decades of unsuccessful searching, Seattle police finally arrested Talbott, 56, in May 2018, though he had not raised suspicions until then. Snohomish County detective Jim Scharf, who led the investigation, credited genetic genealogy for Talbott's capture. The technique first made headlines in 2018 after it was used to find the suspected "Golden State Killer", who is blamed for 12 murders and more than 50 rapes dating back to the mid-1970s. In both cases, as well as at least 70 others that have been solved since, DNA found at the crime scenes was compared with the database at GEDmatch, a free genealogy website. The website allows users to post DNA test results and then generates a list of people with similar genomes, enabling users to find distant relatives. The database also allowed police officers to search through people with similar genetic profiles to DNA found at crime scenes. Tracing back through family trees and isolating common relatives can lead investigators to a suspect. In addition to helping solve more than 70 cases, which had gone unsolved for years, some of the suspects identified through the process were convicted after pleading guilty. But this is the first case in which a trial was organised, despite Talbott maintaining his innocence. After his sentencing yesterday, he continued to claim his innocence and said he intended to appeal the sentence. ------------------------ GENETICS,SCIENCE & SOCIETY Crime solvers embraced genetic genealogy The Golden State killer case was just the beginning BY TINA HESMAN SAEY 8:32AM, DECEMBER 17, 2018 Every week, Ellen Greytak checks DNA profiles in a genealogy database. She’s not searching for long-lost relatives. She’s out to find family members of unknown assailants in rape and murder cases. Greytak is director of bioinformatics at Parabon NanoLabs in Reston, Va. Since May, the company has used genetic genealogy, a forensic technique for tracking down suspects through their family trees, to help close more than a dozen cases nationwide. In 2018, criminal investigators in the United States embraced the tool, solving decades-old cold cases and some fresh crimes. More than 12 million Americans have jumped on the consumer genetic testing bandwagon, sending spit samples to companies like 23andMe or AncestryDNA to learn about health risks and to explore family origins (SN: 6/23/18, p. 26). People who’ve had their DNA tested and want to find relatives tested by a different company can upload their results to a public database called GEDMatch. Now GEDMatch is being used to locate rape and murder suspects. In April, Sacramento police arrested Joseph James DeAngelo as a suspect in the Golden State Killer case (SN Online: 4/29/18). DeAngelo, a former police officer, is accused of committing about 50 rapes and 12 murders from 1974 to 1986. Police found DNA matches in GEDMatch to multiple third cousins of DeAngelo. Building out the suspect’s family tree eventually led investigators to DeAngelo. A few weeks after DeAngelo’s arrest, Parabon identified William Earl Talbott II as a suspect in a 1987 double murder of a young Canadian couple in Snohomish County, Wash. (SN: 6/23/18, p. 11). Since then, suspects in 16 other cases have been arrested after genetic genealogy searches.
